turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**This is a fair-to-good Google L6 offer, but not a compelling “leave a job I like” offer.** I would **negotiate rather than accept or walk away now**.

The main issue is that Google is offering roughly market-level L6 compensation while asking you to:

- Leave a role where you are already happy
- Take a $5,000 base-salary reduction
- Give up Meta equity and future Meta refresh potential
- Accept uncertainty around Google refreshes
- Assume role/team/performance risk

For a passive, happy candidate, I would want a **meaningful switching premium**, not merely equivalent compensation.

## The math

Assuming target bonus, flat stock prices, and no future refresh grants:

| | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $235K |
| Target/expected bonus | $36K | $47K |
| Annualized initial equity | ~$250K current run rate | $270K |
| **Normalized annual TC** | **~$526K** | **~$552K** |

Google’s four-year guaranteed package is:

- Cash over four years: $282K × 4 = **$1.128M**
- Equity: **$1.080M**
- Total: **$2.208M**
- Four-year average: **$552K**

That is only **$26K/year, or about 5%, above your current $526K run rate**.

Your stated Meta vesting over the next 12 months is only $200K, making your next-year Meta compensation approximately **$476K**. Google therefore looks much better in the immediate term. But the four-year economics matter more when evaluating a career move.

### Important: confirm the vesting schedule

Recent independent reporting says Google’s standard new-hire GSU schedule is commonly front-loaded at **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, while refresh grants generally vest evenly. Your actual award documents control, so confirm this in writing. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule))

If your $1.08M grant uses 38/32/20/10, the Google package looks like:

| Year | Equity vesting | Approx. TC |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410.4K | **$692.4K** |
| 2 | $345.6K | **$627.6K** |
| 3 | $216K | **$498K** |
| 4 | $108K | **$390K** |

That front-loading is great initially, but it creates a substantial **year-four cliff** unless refreshes fill it.

Treat refreshes as upside, not part of the offer. Google’s own description says equity refresh amounts depend on modeled recommendations, performance, location, role and managerial discretion. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

## Is it market-competitive?

Yes. Current reported data puts:

- Bay Area Google L6 PM median TC around **$551K**
- US L6 PM median base around **$240K**
- US L6 median annual stock around **$230K**
- US L6 median TC around **$514K**, with a reported 90th percentile around **$671K** ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

So your offer is approximately:

- **At the Bay Area L6 median in four-year annualized TC**
- Slightly below median base
- Above median initial-grant equity on an annualized basis
- Not unusually generous for an L6 passive recruit

Google currently posts comparable Bay Area Senior PM roles with base ranges reaching roughly the high $270Ks plus a 20% target bonus and equity, so asking materially above $235K is reasonable. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS))

## What I would ask for

### Opening request

Ask for:

- **Base: $265K–$270K**
- **New-hire equity: $1.30M–$1.35M**
- **Sign-on bonus: $100K**
- Confirmation in writing of:
  - Exact new-hire vesting schedule
  - Vesting commencement date
  - First vest date
  - First annual-refresh eligibility date

A clean specific request would be:

> **$265K base, $1.30M in new-hire equity, and a $100K sign-on bonus.**

At a 20% target bonus, that package would average approximately:

- Base and bonus: $318K/year
- Four-year cash: $1.272M
- Equity: $1.30M
- Sign-on: $100K
- Four-year total: **$2.672M**
- Four-year average: **$668K**

That is an aggressive anchor, but not absurd: it is roughly around the reported upper end of L6 compensation, and you are a successful Meta IC6 who was recruited rather than an active candidate. ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/))

### A strong settlement

I would consider this a good result:

- **Base: $255K–$260K**
- **Equity: $1.20M–$1.25M**
- **Sign-on: $50K–$100K**

For example, $255K base, $1.20M equity and a $75K sign-on produces:

- $306K annual target cash
- $1.224M four-year cash
- $1.20M equity
- $75K sign-on
- **$2.499M total, or about $625K/year**

That is roughly a **19% premium** over your current $526K run rate—much more appropriate for leaving a job you like.

### My compensation floor

If compensation matters heavily and the role itself is not clearly superior, I would want approximately:

- **At least $250K base**
- **At least $1.20M equity**
- Preferably **$50K+ sign-on**

That combination is approximately $600K–$613K annualized over four years, depending on the sign-on. It creates a 14%–17% switching premium over your current run rate.

If they stay near **$235K / $1.08M / $0**, I would probably remain at Meta unless the Google role is materially better for your trajectory, scope, manager, or personal interests.

## How to frame the negotiation

Do not frame it as “market data says I deserve more.” Your strongest argument is **opportunity cost and switching threshold**.

You can say:

> I’m very excited about the team and appreciate the offer. I also want to be transparent that I wasn’t actively looking and I’m happy at Meta, so leaving requires a meaningful premium over my current position and the equity I would be walking away from.
>
> My current annual compensation is approximately $526K, including about $250K per year in equity, and I have approximately $200K vesting over the next 12 months. The current offer annualizes to roughly $552K over four years before any non-guaranteed refreshes, with a lower base salary and no sign-on.
>
> To make the move compelling, I’d be looking for approximately **$265K in base, $1.30M in new-hire equity, and a $100K sign-on bonus**. I’m flexible on the mix if there are constraints between base, equity and sign-on, but I’d need the guaranteed four-year value to move materially closer to that level.

Then stop talking and let the recruiter respond.

If they say base is constrained:

> Understood. If base flexibility is limited, could the difference be addressed through additional new-hire equity and a sign-on bonus?

If they say refreshes will solve the cliff:

> I understand refreshes are part of the compensation program, but because they aren’t guaranteed, I need to evaluate the decision based primarily on the written offer. Could you increase the initial grant to account for that uncertainty?

## Additional questions before accepting

Ask for concrete answers to these:

1. **Is the $1.08M converted to shares based on a trailing average price or the price on a particular date?**
2. **What is the exact vesting schedule—38/32/20/10 or something else?**
3. **When is the first vest, especially relative to your Meta vest dates?**
4. **When would you first be eligible for an equity refresh?**
5. **Would joining after a compensation-cycle cutoff delay your first refresh?**
6. **What has the team’s L6 refresh range historically looked like at meets/exceeds ratings?**  
   Treat any answer as illustrative, not guaranteed.
7. **Is the annual bonus prorated in your first calendar year?**
8. **Can the start date be moved until immediately after an important Meta vest?**

Start-date timing can be worth tens of thousands of dollars and may be easier for the recruiter to accommodate than additional compensation.

## Recommendation

**Negotiate. Do not accept the current offer immediately.**

My decision rule would be:

- **$625K+ four-year annualized guaranteed value:** strong financial reason to accept, assuming you like the role.
- **$600K–$625K:** reasonable; decide based on team, trajectory and manager.
- **$552K–$575K:** fair market offer, but probably not enough to leave a job you like.
- **No meaningful improvement:** politely decline and stay at Meta.

The current offer is not a lowball. But it is a **market offer**, whereas your circumstances justify asking for a **poaching offer**.

turns.user: Update: I told the recruiter I'd be walking away from about $200,000 of RSUs that would vest in the next 12 months. Final offer: base $240,000, RSUs stay at $1,080,000, plus a $200,000 sign-on bonus. They said this is their best offer. Should I take it?
turns.reply:
## My take: **lean accept—assuming you like the role and manager**

I would **not walk away over compensation anymore**. The revised offer is financially strong enough to justify the move, though it is not such an overwhelming windfall that you should ignore role quality or career risk.

### Revised economics

Assuming target bonus and valuing the RSUs at grant value:

|  | Google |
|---|---:|
| Base | $240K |
| Target bonus | $48K |
| Annualized new-hire RSUs | $270K |
| **Recurring annualized TC** | **$558K** |
| Sign-on | $200K |
| **Four-year total** | **$2.432M** |
| **Four-year average** | **$608K/year** |

Against your current Meta run rate:

- Meta: approximately **$526K/year**
- Google including sign-on amortized over four years: **$608K/year**
- Premium: approximately **$82K/year**
- Four-year premium: approximately **$328K**, or **15.6%**

Current self-reported market data puts Bay Area Google L6 PM median compensation at about **$606K**, so the final package is approximately market-median for that level—not extraordinary for Google L6, but clearly competitive. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## Why the $200K matters

The original offer gave you only about a 5% four-year premium. That was inadequate for leaving a position you liked.

The sign-on changes the equation because it:

1. Fully replaces the approximately $200K of near-term Meta equity you identified.
2. Is cash rather than additional four-year equity.
3. Raises the four-year premium to approximately 16%.
4. Reduces the financial risk of switching employers.

Assuming 25% of Google’s grant vests in year one, your approximate first-year compensation would be:

- $240K base
- $48K target bonus
- $270K Google RSUs
- $200K sign-on
- **Total: $758K**

Compared with approximately **$476K** from Meta over the next 12 months based on the $200K vesting figure you provided.

The actual first-year figure will depend on Google’s exact vesting schedule, bonus proration, start date, and stock-price movement.

## The biggest caveat

The Google package’s **recurring** annualized value is only about **$558K**, versus your current Meta run rate of $526K—a recurring premium of just **$32K, or 6%**.

Therefore:

- The first four years look good because of the sign-on.
- Long-term compensation will depend materially on Google refresh grants.
- Because refreshes are not guaranteed, don’t assume you will permanently earn $608K or more.
- If the initial grant is front-loaded, the later-year compensation cliff may be substantial.

This means I would accept because the compensation now adequately supports a move—not because Google is necessarily going to pay dramatically more forever.

## When I would take it

I would accept if all of these are true:

- You are genuinely interested in the product area.
- The hiring manager seems at least as good as your Meta manager.
- The scope is appropriate for L6 and offers credible L7 growth.
- You are comfortable with Google’s performance-management environment and team stability.
- You expect to remain long enough to avoid repaying the sign-on.
- The commute and office expectations are acceptable.

If those conditions are satisfied, **the financial package clears a reasonable switching threshold**.

## When I would stay at Meta

Stay if:

- You clearly prefer your current manager, team, or product.
- The Google role is less strategic or has ambiguous scope.
- You suspect it is an L6 role with limited path to L7.
- You are likely to leave Google within the sign-on repayment period.
- Meta is likely to give you a major refresh or promotion soon.
- Your only reason for moving is compensation and you would regret leaving once the sign-on is spent.

Because you are happy at Meta, Google should not win merely by matching compensation. But a 16% four-year premium is enough that the decision can reasonably turn on the role rather than requiring Google to bid higher.

## Verify these terms before signing

Since they have said it is final, I would not make another broad monetary counter. I would ask for written clarification of:

1. **Sign-on payment schedule**
   - Is all $200K paid immediately?
   - Is any portion deferred until year two?

2. **Clawback**
   - Is repayment required for 12 months, 24 months, or longer?
   - Is repayment prorated or all-or-nothing?
   - What happens if Google terminates you or eliminates the role?
   - Must you repay the gross $200K even though you received less after withholding?

3. **RSU schedule**
   - Exact percentage vesting in each year
   - First vest date
   - Grant-pricing methodology
   - Whether the nominal $1.08M could convert into a materially different number of shares depending on the pricing date

4. **First-year bonus**
   - Whether it is prorated
   - Whether you will participate in the next bonus cycle
   - Whether any minimum bonus is guaranteed

5. **Refresh eligibility**
   - The first compensation cycle in which you are eligible
   - Whether your start date could cause you to miss a cycle

### Tax caution

The $200K is taxable wage income, not a tax-free reimbursement for forfeited RSUs. Federal withholding on separately paid supplemental wages may be 22%, but withholding is only a prepayment and could be below your actual marginal tax liability. California also treats bonuses as wage income. Plan for a possible tax shortfall rather than spending the full net payment. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p505?utm_source=openai))

## Recommendation

**Accept if the Google role is at least roughly as attractive as your Meta role.**

I would characterize the final offer as:

- **Good enough to accept:** yes
- **Financially compelling:** moderately
- **An exceptional Google L6 package:** no
- **Worth leaving a good job you clearly prefer:** probably not
- **Worth leaving for a role you find equally or more attractive:** yes

The recruiter effectively addressed your strongest objection dollar-for-dollar. Unless there is a meaningful role, manager, scope, or clawback concern, I would take the offer.
